title: Study of Acids, Bases and Salts
tagline: Explore properties, reactions and preparation of acids, bases and salts.

overview.intro: Acids, bases and salts are fundamental classes of compounds studied through their definitions, characteristic properties and reactions. This chapter covers common laboratory acids and alkalis, indicators, pH ideas at an introductory level, reactions with metals, carbonates and oxides, neutralisation, and methods of preparing salts. A clear grasp of these concepts supports practical chemistry, equation writing and reasoning about everyday substances.

learningOutcomes: Define acids, bases and alkalis using ionic ideas and common examples.
Describe properties and reactions of acids and bases including indicator changes.
Explain neutralisation and write balanced equations for typical reactions.
Classify salts and outline common laboratory methods of salt preparation.
Apply knowledge to identify substances and predict reaction products.

blocks.text: Acids are substances that produce hydrogen ions, H+, in aqueous solution (often represented as hydronium ions, H3O+). Common mineral acids include hydrochloric acid, sulphuric acid and nitric acid, while organic acids such as acetic acid occur in vinegar. Acids have sour taste in dilute form, turn blue litmus red, and show characteristic pH values below 7.

Dilute acids react with active metals to liberate hydrogen gas, with metal carbonates and bicarbonates to liberate carbon dioxide, and with bases to form salt and water. Concentrated acids may show additional oxidising or dehydrating behaviour depending on the acid, but at this level the focus is on general ionic reactions in solution.

items: Acidic solutions conduct electricity due to presence of ions.
Strength of an acid relates to degree of ionisation in water, not just concentration.
Indicators such as litmus, methyl orange and phenolphthalein show distinct colours in acids.
Always add acid to water carefully when diluting, not the reverse, for safety.

blocks.text: Bases are metal oxides or hydroxides that react with acids to form salt and water. Alkalis are bases that are soluble in water and produce hydroxide ions, OH−, in solution; examples include sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide. Ammonium hydroxide is an important alkali formed when ammonia dissolves in water.

Alkalis have a bitter taste and soapy feel, turn red litmus blue, and have pH values above 7. They react with acids in neutralisation, with some ammonium salts on warming to release ammonia gas, and with solutions of certain metal salts to precipitate insoluble hydroxides.

items.note: A typical neutralisation producing a neutral salt.
Formation of an insoluble metal hydroxide precipitate.

blocks.text: Indicators are substances that change colour in acidic and alkaline media, helping to identify the nature of a solution or detect the end point of neutralisation. Litmus turns red in acid and blue in alkali; methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali; phenolphthalein is colourless in acid and pink in alkali.

Neutralisation is the reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water. In ionic terms for strong acid and strong alkali, H+ ions combine with OH− ions to form water. The resulting solution may be neutral, acidic or alkaline depending on the nature of the acid and base involved.

learn.title: Salts: Types and Methods of Preparation

blocks.text: A salt is formed when the replaceable hydrogen of an acid is wholly or partly replaced by a metal ion or ammonium ion. Normal salts result from complete replacement (e.g. NaCl), acid salts from partial replacement in polybasic acids (e.g. NaHSO4), and basic salts from incomplete neutralisation of a base in specific cases.

Laboratory preparation of salts depends on solubility. Soluble salts may be prepared by neutralisation followed by crystallisation, by action of acid on metal, carbonate or insoluble base, while insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation (double decomposition) and then filtered, washed and dried.

items.meaning: A salt formed by complete replacement of replaceable hydrogen of an acid.
A salt formed by partial replacement of replaceable hydrogen of a polybasic acid.
Formation of an insoluble solid when two solutions react.

blocks.text: Acids react with metal oxides to give salt and water, showing the basic nature of metal oxides. Bases react with non-metal oxides in some cases to form salts and water, reflecting acidic character of certain non-metal oxides. These reactions reinforce classification of oxides and help in writing balanced chemical equations.

In daily life and industry, neutralisation is used in treating acidity, adjusting soil pH, and handling alkaline or acidic wastes. Understanding salt preparation is essential for obtaining pure samples in the laboratory and for recognising why a particular method is chosen for a given salt.

items: Choose preparation method based on whether the desired salt is soluble or insoluble.
Use excess insoluble reactant when appropriate to ensure complete reaction of acid.
Crystallisation yields solid salt from a saturated solution on cooling or evaporation.
Wash precipitates to remove soluble impurities before drying.

keyPoints: Acids produce H+ ions in aqueous solution; alkalis produce OH− ions.
Indicators change colour depending on acidic or alkaline nature of a solution.
Neutralisation between acid and base forms salt and water.
Salts may be normal or acid salts depending on replacement of hydrogen in the acid.
Soluble salts can be prepared by reaction with acids followed by crystallisation.
Insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation and separated by filtration.
Acids react with active metals, carbonates and bases to give characteristic products.
Alkalis react with acids and with solutions of some metal salts to form precipitates.
Method of salt preparation depends on solubility and reactivity of reactants.
Balanced equations and correct reagent choice are essential in practical chemistry.
examFocus: Define acid, base, alkali and salt with correct ionic or compositional ideas.
Recall indicator colour changes and use them to identify solutions.
Write balanced equations for neutralisation and common acid reactions.
Select an appropriate method to prepare a named soluble or insoluble salt.
Distinguish normal and acid salts with examples.
Explain observations such as gas evolution or precipitate formation.
Use correct laboratory terms: filtrate, residue, crystallisation, precipitation.

A compound formed when replaceable hydrogen of an acid is replaced by a metal or ammonium ion.

questions.prompt: An acid in aqueous solution produces:
questions.answer: H+ ions
questions.explanation: Acids are characterised by production of hydrogen ions in water.
questions.commonMistake: Hydroxide ions are produced by alkalis, not acids.

questions.prompt: Which indicator turns pink in an alkaline solution?
questions.answer: Phenolphthalein
questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic solution and pink in alkaline solution.
questions.commonMistake: Methyl orange turns yellow in alkali, not pink.

questions.prompt: The reaction between an acid and a base to form salt and water is called:
questions.answer: neutralisation
questions.explanation: Neutralisation involves combination of H+ and OH− ions to form water along with a salt.
questions.commonMistake: Precipitation forms an insoluble solid, which is different from neutralisation.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an alkali?
questions.answer: Sodium hydroxide
questions.explanation: An alkali is a base soluble in water; sodium hydroxide dissolves to give OH− ions.
questions.commonMistake: Not all bases are alkalis; solubility in water matters.

questions.prompt: An insoluble salt is best prepared by:
questions.answer: precipitation
questions.explanation: Mixing suitable solutions forms an insoluble salt that can be filtered and washed.
questions.commonMistake: Crystallisation is used for soluble salts, not insoluble ones.

questions.prompt: A solution turns blue litmus red. It is likely to be:
questions.answer: acidic
questions.explanation: Acids turn blue litmus paper red.
questions.commonMistake: Alkalis turn red litmus blue, the opposite change.

questions.prompt: NaHSO4 is an example of a:
questions.answer: acid salt
questions.explanation: NaHSO4 retains replaceable hydrogen, showing partial replacement in sulphuric acid.
questions.commonMistake: A normal salt of sulphuric acid would have no replaceable hydrogen left.

questions.prompt: Which reaction produces carbon dioxide gas?
questions.answer: Acid + metal carbonate
questions.explanation: Carbonates react with acids to form salt, water and carbon dioxide gas.
questions.commonMistake: Acid-alkali neutralisation produces water, not carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: A base soluble in water is called an ________.
questions.answer: alkali
questions.explanation: Alkalis are soluble bases that furnish hydroxide ions in aqueous solution.
questions.commonMistake: Do not use base and alkali as identical terms.

questions.prompt: The insoluble solid formed in a precipitation reaction is called a ________.
questions.answer: precipitate
questions.explanation: A precipitate separates out when an insoluble product forms in solution.
questions.commonMistake: The clear liquid above a settled precipitate is the supernatant, not the precipitate.

questions.prompt: Methyl orange turns ________ in an acidic solution.
questions.answer: red
questions.explanation: Methyl orange is red in acid and yellow in alkali.
questions.commonMistake: Remember the opposite colours for phenolphthalein in acid and alkali.

questions.prompt: Define neutralisation.
questions.answer: Neutralisation is the chemical reaction in which an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water.
questions.explanation: In ionic terms, hydrogen ions combine with hydroxide ions to form water.
questions.commonMistake: Include both products: salt and water.

questions.prompt: State the colour changes of litmus in acid and alkali.
questions.answer: Blue litmus turns red in an acidic solution, while red litmus turns blue in an alkaline solution.
questions.explanation: Litmus provides a simple test for acidic or alkaline nature.
questions.commonMistake: Specify which colour litmus paper you start with when stating the change.

questions.prompt: How would you prepare a pure sample of copper(II) sulphate crystals from copper(II) oxide and dilute sulphuric acid?
questions.answer: Warm dilute sulphuric acid and add copper(II) oxide in small portions until some remains unreacted, ensuring all acid is used. Filter to remove excess oxide, then heat the filtrate to obtain a saturated solution and allow it to cool so that copper(II) sulphate crystals form. Dry the crystals between filter papers.
questions.explanation: Using excess insoluble base prevents contamination with unreacted acid and crystallisation gives the solid salt.
questions.commonMistake: Do not evaporate to complete dryness if hydrated crystals are required.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between a normal salt and an acid salt with one example each.
questions.answer: A normal salt is formed when all replaceable hydrogen atoms of an acid are replaced by metal or ammonium ions, for example sodium chloride (NaCl) from HCl. An acid salt is formed when only part of the replaceable hydrogen of a polybasic acid is replaced, for example sodium hydrogen sulphate (NaHSO4) from H2SO4.
questions.explanation: The distinction depends on whether replaceable hydrogen remains in the salt.
questions.commonMistake: Acid salts are associated with polybasic acids, not all acids.

questions.prompt: Describe the reactions of dilute hydrochloric acid with (i) zinc, (ii) sodium carbonate, and (iii) sodium hydroxide, including products.
questions.answer: (i) Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form zinc chloride and hydrogen gas: Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl2 + H2. (ii) Sodium carbonate reacts to form sodium chloride, water and carbon dioxide: Na2CO3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H2O + CO2. (iii) Sodium hydroxide neutralises the acid to form sodium chloride and water: NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O. These reactions illustrate typical behaviour of acids with metals, carbonates and alkalis.
questions.explanation: Each class of reactant gives characteristic products that help identify substances.
questions.commonMistake: Balance equations and include correct gaseous products where formed.

questions.prompt: Explain how you would prepare lead(II) sulphate in the laboratory, stating the principle and steps.
questions.answer: Lead(II) sulphate is insoluble, so it is prepared by precipitation. Mix aqueous solutions of a soluble lead(II) salt such as lead(II) nitrate and a soluble sulphate such as sodium sulphate to form a white precipitate of lead(II) sulphate: Pb(NO3)2 + Na2SO4 → PbSO4↓ + 2NaNO3. Filter the mixture to collect the precipitate, wash it with distilled water to remove soluble impurities, and dry it.
questions.explanation: Double decomposition gives an insoluble salt when appropriate ions are brought together in solution.
questions.commonMistake: Do not choose crystallisation for an insoluble salt.

questions.prompt: Discuss the choice of method for preparing (i) sodium chloride, (ii) zinc sulphate, and (iii) barium sulphate, giving reasons.
questions.answer: (i) Sodium chloride, a soluble salt, can be prepared by neutralising hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide solution and crystallising the product, because both reactants are soluble and the end point can be detected. (ii) Zinc sulphate, also soluble, can be prepared by reacting dilute sulphuric acid with excess zinc or zinc oxide, filtering off excess solid, and crystallising the filtrate. (iii) Barium sulphate is insoluble and is prepared by precipitation, for example by mixing barium chloride solution with sodium sulphate solution, followed by filtration, washing and drying. The method in each case depends on solubility and suitable reactants.
questions.explanation: Correct method selection ensures purity and practicality of preparation.
questions.commonMistake: Match each salt to a method consistent with its solubility.

questions.prompt: A colourless solution turns phenolphthalein pink and methyl orange yellow. Identify the nature of the solution and explain.
questions.answer: The solution is alkaline. Phenolphthalein becomes pink in alkaline medium, and methyl orange becomes yellow in alkaline medium (it is red in acid). Both indicator results consistently indicate the presence of a base/alkali in solution.
questions.explanation: Using two indicators provides confirmatory evidence of the solution’s nature.
questions.commonMistake: Interpret each indicator colour in the correct medium.

questions.prompt: A student adds dilute sulphuric acid to excess copper(II) carbonate, filters the mixture and evaporates the filtrate. Identify the salt formed and justify each step.
questions.answer: The salt formed is copper(II) sulphate. Dilute sulphuric acid reacts with copper(II) carbonate to produce copper(II) sulphate, water and carbon dioxide. Using excess carbonate ensures all acid reacts, avoiding acidic contamination. Filtration removes unreacted solid carbonate, and evaporation/crystallisation of the filtrate yields copper(II) sulphate crystals.
questions.explanation: Each step has a purpose: complete reaction, separation of excess reactant, and recovery of soluble salt.
questions.commonMistake: If acid were in excess, the filtrate would be contaminated and unsafe to crystallise as pure salt.

questions.prompt: Given three unlabelled solutions—dilute HCl, NaOH and NaCl—describe tests using indicators and one chemical test to identify each.
questions.answer: First test each solution with litmus: HCl turns blue litmus red (acidic), NaOH turns red litmus blue (alkaline), and NaCl shows no change (neutral). To confirm HCl, add a small amount of sodium carbonate solution; effervescence of carbon dioxide indicates an acid. To confirm NaOH, add a few drops to copper(II) sulphate solution to obtain a blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide. The solution showing neutral indicator behaviour and no such reactions is NaCl.
questions.explanation: A combination of indicator and characteristic reactions allows reliable identification.
questions.commonMistake: Use safe, small-scale tests and do not rely on taste or touch.

questions.prompt: Why is it unsuitable to prepare sodium sulphate by adding sodium metal to dilute sulphuric acid in the laboratory? Suggest a better method.
questions.answer: Sodium metal reacts violently with acids and water, making the reaction dangerous and difficult to control in the laboratory. A better method is to neutralise dilute sulphuric acid with sodium hydroxide solution (or sodium carbonate) using an indicator to reach the end point, then crystallise the solution to obtain sodium sulphate.
questions.explanation: Choice of reactants must consider safety as well as chemical suitability.
questions.commonMistake: Even if chemically possible, highly reactive metals are not appropriate laboratory reagents for salt preparation.
